newsitem.title: UK: Belgian bonds outperform in latest week - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: Belgian bonds outperform in latest week - Salomon.

text.p: Belgian bonds performed best in a week which saw positive returns for most government bond markets, according to the Salomon Brothers world government bond index.

Domestic buying of Belgian bonds took the market higher, despite allegations, later denied, that the Treasury had massaged Belgium's debt position to improve its chances of qualifying for European Economic and Monetary Union.
Belgain bonds provided a return of 0.79 percent in local currency terms, as the overall bond index gained 0.41 percent.

Still at the core of Europe, Dutch and German bonds were only narrowly beaten into second place, providing a return of 0.78 percent. French bonds were also up there with the winners, gaining 0.77 percent in local terms.
The worst performers in local terms were Canadian bonds which were the only ones in the index to lose ground, dropping 0.32 percent in the week.
Analysts said Japanese investors were repatriating money out of North America, as the Japanese stock market sustained heavy losses. Japanese bonds gained 0.50 percent in yen terms.
Swiss bonds made a meagre gain of 0.16 percent, while U.S. Treasuries only just outperformed them with a gain of 0.17 percent.
British gilts and Italian BTPs put in a mediocre performance, gaining 0.43 percent and 0.26 percent respectively.
But in dollar terms, gilts were strong, coming in as the second best performer with a return of 0.63 percent.
Canadian bonds far outstripped other markets in dollar terms, climbing 1.37 percent as currency gains outweighed selling pressure on the market.
The other gainers were the U.S. at 0.17 percent, and Japan at 0.14 percent.
In dollar terms, the biggest loser was Austria, which shed 1.69 percent of its value this week. France dropped 1.50 percent, and Germany lost 1.38 percent.

Salomon's bond index is calculated using all government bonds with over one year to maturity, weighted for market capitalisation. Only bonds freely available to institutional investors and with a certain minimum amount outstanding are included. Returns take account of price moves and accrued interest.
